rationale: #971. A declarator wrapped in parentheses is legal C that means nothing but grouping, but the grammar gives the grouping its own node, so the declared name sits under `parenthesized_declarator`. That parent type was missing from the declaration-parent list, so the name was classified as a READ OF ITSELF and published as `uses global -> grouped_name` -- from the same occurrence that also emitted the function symbol. Wrong (a declaration is not a read) and redundant. Measured: 109 spurious `uses` edges removed across 2,498 corpus files, corpus evidence redis/deps/lua/src/lauxlib.c:229 `LUALIB_API void (luaL_register) (...)`. The control is the body reads of the SAME names, which must still be published -- otherwise the fix has only moved the gate. The fix distinguishes GROUPING from a function POINTER by what the parens contain: a pointer_declarator inside means pointer-to-function (a variable), anything else means grouping (a function). `grouped_pointer` is the control that keeps that distinction honest -- it must stay a variable.

expectSymbols.name: grouped_pointer
expectSymbols.comment: CORRECTION, and the point of the whole fix: `int (*(grouped_pointer))(int n);` is a genuine function POINTER -- the parens contain a pointer_declarator -- so it is a variable, not a function. The pre-#971 test keyed on the parentheses alone and got BOTH shapes wrong: it published grouped prototypes as variables AND would have had no way to tell this one apart. The fix tests what the parens CONTAIN.

expectRelationships.comment: A real call of a parenthesised-declarator function. The fix suppresses only the DECLARING occurrence; the call site is untouched.
CONTROL: a genuine read of a parenthesised-declarator name inside a body. If this edge disappears the fix over-suppressed.

forbidRelationships.comment: THE defect #971 fixes. The declaring occurrence is a declaration, not a read of itself.
Same, for the parenthesised POINTER declarator -- the deepest shape, where the identifier sits two levels under function_declarator.
Same, with a void return type.
Same on a PROTOTYPE rather than a definition -- the shape the corpus evidence actually had (lauxlib.c:229).
